40% of Instinct users give the agent a credit card within 3 weeks    

And once someone trusts it with something sensitive, they stay (retention hits ~80%)    

Noah on earning consumer trust and protecting user data:    

"It takes several weeks to build trust and I actually don't have a problem with that, because one of the core principles on our end is the user should always be in control of their data.     

They should share data with Instinct at the rate at which they feel comfortable with. And if they wanna take it back, they can certainly take it back.    

Within three weeks 40% of the user base is giving Instinct access to a credit card autonomously to be able to purchase theoretically anywhere.    

There are systems that we've put in place that are detached from Instinct, the agent architecture itself, that are put in place to be proactive about these things and to decouple the risk.     

Any piece of content, any piece of text, anything that might be consumed by Instinct goes through what we call these firewalls, which can intercept, can reject, can block malicious pieces of content coming in and trying to convince Instinct to do something.    

For every action that Instinct might take, or for every thought that it might have, that is being actively monitored by a system that is decoupled from Instinct itself, which is able to pause it, intercept it, to approve or disapprove of what might happen next before it takes the action.     

There's just so much more under the hood that is put in place to enable the agent to be as capable as possible, but also safe and trustworthy."

A list of surprising and mind-boggling stats from this conversation:

- $1B+ a year in transaction volume (still invite only)

- Growing 10%+ A DAY and has spent zero dollars on marketing

- 40% of users shared a personal credit card with Instinct within 3 weeks

- Instinct launched to about 200 friends and family

- Invites have sold on eBay for around $300

- More than 50% of Instinct's traffic doesn't run on iMessage

- Instinct has proactively called Noah three times

- The company is less than a year old

- Noah is 23

I don't just love how these businesses are bringing more transparency and trust to their tokens and underlying businesses through external audits. I also love how aggressively the market reacts to it.

Interestingly, there's a ton of interesting crypto businesses out there all sitting in the same boat: genuinely compelling value proposition, already doing decent revenue from real world clients and users, but the token doesn't move an inch because people either don't trust it or don't even know it exists.

I think there's a massive opportunity here for those actually willing to put in the work, dig deep to find these businesses, and do the diligence on how committed these teams really are to their token. Do that, and you can front-run massive repricings before the market wakes up.

As more transparency and initiatives like Blockworks TTF become the standard, I expect this opportunity to fade and the market to get more efficient at pricing in offchain revenue too. But for the next 1-2 years, this is literally a window of free money.

In AI, if you want people to switch, you have to leapfrog.

Meta had Meta AI everywhere: WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook. Incredible distribution. But yet another chatbot, even one that’s 10% better, probably wasn’t going to pull people away from ChatGPT.

Muse is a much bigger jump. Give the agent its own computer, let it keep working when you close the app, and make the model fast and cheap enough that you can actually use it all day especially for a new use case (buying stuff for you). Instinct is pushing in that direction too. This week I sent more queries to Muse than ChatGPT, which I would not have expected a month ago.

Now what happens when ChatGPT ships the same experience this week? You have to leapfrog again. Software product advantages get copied fast.

My bet is that the durable advantage underneath all this is the model: how good it is, how fast it is, and what it costs to run. If you don’t own the weights, you’re building on someone else’s cost curve and you can’t compete with them. 

And beneath the model is compute. Compute lets you train a better model, serve it cheaply, and keep it available as usage explodes. 

IMO one can tell a pretty compelling story about who wins this market just by looking at who has compute today, and who will have it in two years.
